name: Book Nook
imageAlt: Book Nook's forest-green homepage with its book-sharing hero and new arrivals
summary: A community library for discovering, sharing, borrowing, and returning books.
evidence: JWT-protected APIs, ownership checks, and a complete borrow / return workflow.
overview: Book Nook connects readers with books shared by a community. I built a Next.js and TypeScript frontend alongside a separate Express API, with MongoDB storing books and borrowing records. Readers can discover titles, contribute their own books, and manage loans through personal dashboards.
challenge: Connect an inviting reading experience to real application rules: who can change a book, whether a copy is available, and which borrowing records belong to the signed-in reader.
solution: I separated the interface from the Express API, used Better Auth for sessions and JWTs, and checked identity and ownership on protected endpoints. Borrow and return operations update availability, while the dashboard makes loan information easier to follow.
features: Book discovery with search, categories, and sorting
Add, edit, and delete your own books
Borrow available copies and track due dates
Return books and restore available copies
Image uploads, reader profiles, and dark/light themes

architecture.title: One product. Two connected applications.
architecture.description: A simplified view of the application boundary—not a claim that every request takes the same route.

nodes.label: 01 / INTERFACE
nodes.title: Next.js + TypeScript
nodes.detail: Catalog, forms, dashboards, and protected pages.

nodes.label: 02 / IDENTITY
nodes.title: Better Auth + JWT
nodes.detail: Sessions identify readers; bearer tokens accompany protected API requests.

nodes.label: 03 / API
nodes.title: Express + jose
nodes.detail: JWKS token verification, ownership checks, and book / borrow endpoints.

nodes.label: 04 / DATA
nodes.title: MongoDB
nodes.detail: Book documents, available copies, and user-scoped borrowing records.

architecture.note: Authentication answers who is making the request. Ownership checks decide which records that person may change.

workflow.title: Discover
workflow.detail: Browse the catalog and narrow it down by title, author, or category.

workflow.title: Sign in
workflow.detail: Authenticate before using protected pages and borrowing actions.

workflow.title: Borrow
workflow.detail: The API conditionally decreases an available copy and creates a dated borrowing record.

workflow.title: Return
workflow.detail: The API checks the borrower, removes the loan record, and restores an available copy.

decisions.title: Verify identity at the API boundary
decisions.choice: Bearer JWTs verified against Better Auth's JWKS with jose, including issuer and audience checks.
decisions.reason: A protected page is not a substitute for protecting the endpoint that reads or changes data.
decisions.tradeoff: The separate frontend and API need consistent auth configuration and reachable signing keys.

decisions.title: Scope writes to the owner
decisions.choice: Update and delete queries match both the book ID and the authenticated owner's email.
decisions.reason: Being signed in should not allow a reader to change someone else's contribution.
decisions.tradeoff: A stable user ID would be a stronger long-term ownership key than an email address.

decisions.title: Check availability when updating
decisions.choice: The copy decrement matches only a book whose copies are greater than zero.
decisions.reason: Checking availability inside the update is better than relying on a possibly stale interface.
decisions.tradeoff: The copy update and loan insert are separate writes; a transaction is a future consistency improvement.

lessons: Connecting separate Next.js and Express deployments
Designing feedback around asynchronous forms and API actions
improvements: Transactional borrow / return operations and stronger server validation
Borrowing history, pagination, and automated API tests
Due-date reminders and a clearer overdue policy

name: Bazar Dor
imageAlt: Bazar Dor homepage showing Bengali market prices and product cards
summary: A Bengali-language guide to everyday market prices in Bangladesh.
evidence: Localized data presentation, market comparisons, and session-protected details.
overview: Bazar Dor brings essential commodity prices together in one approachable Bengali interface. Visitors can browse products by category, follow price increases and decreases, and compare prices across markets. Registered users can explore detailed product information and manage their profiles.
challenge: Make changing market prices easy to scan and compare without losing the local context that makes the information useful.
solution: I designed a responsive product directory with price-change indicators, category browsing and sorting, detailed market comparisons, and account-based access to deeper product data.
features: Daily price changes and a scrolling price ticker
Category browsing, sorting, and product details
Market-wise comparisons and estimated price ranges
Email and social sign-in with protected pages

architecture.title: External prices. Local context.
architecture.description: Product prices come from an external API. MongoDB supports authentication data, not a custom market-price collection.

nodes.label: 01 / SOURCE
nodes.title: Product API
nodes.detail: External product, category, and market-price information.

nodes.label: 02 / APPLICATION
nodes.title: Next.js
nodes.detail: Server-rendered pages and session checks for protected details.

nodes.label: 03 / PRESENTATION
nodes.title: Bengali interface
nodes.detail: Sorting, change indicators, localized numbers, and market summaries.

nodes.label: 04 / IDENTITY
nodes.title: Better Auth
nodes.detail: Email / social sign-in with authentication records in MongoDB.

architecture.note: The cards show application responsibilities. Better Auth is a supporting identity layer, not the destination of product-price data.

workflow.title: Scan
workflow.detail: See the biggest upward and downward price changes on the homepage.

workflow.title: Browse
workflow.detail: Choose a category and sort products by the current price.

workflow.title: Authenticate
workflow.detail: A server-side session check protects the detailed product view.

workflow.title: Compare
workflow.detail: Inspect market ranges and the minimum, maximum, and estimated average.

decisions.title: Design for Bengali readers
decisions.choice: Bengali labels, localized numeric formatting, and familiar product categories.
decisions.reason: Market information should be understandable without requiring readers to translate the interface.
decisions.tradeoff: Responsive layouts need room for longer labels and locally formatted values.

decisions.title: Explain a range, not a false exact price
decisions.choice: Display market minimums, maximums, and an average of market midpoints.
decisions.reason: A range communicates that prices differ between markets.
decisions.tradeoff: The average is an estimate from supplied ranges, not a weighted transaction average.

decisions.title: Check sessions on the server
decisions.choice: Use Better Auth's session API before rendering protected product details.
decisions.reason: Protected content should not depend on a client-side visibility check.
decisions.tradeoff: Account access adds a step to the comparison journey; public summaries remain browsable.

lessons: Turning external API data into useful summaries
Combining server-rendered content with client-side sorting
improvements: Pagination and more resilient API error states
Tests for price calculations and account flows

name: FitLog
imageAlt: FitLog workout library with exercise cards and a dark interface
summary: A workout library that turns exercise discovery into a practical daily plan.
evidence: Shared React state, persistent plans, and derived workout summaries.
overview: FitLog is a workout companion for exploring exercises and making a plan that sticks. Users can inspect individual workouts, assemble a daily routine, save exercises for later, and track completed work. Plans persist locally so they are still there after a refresh.
challenge: Give people a simple way to move from browsing exercises to organizing an achievable workout session.
solution: I connected a searchable exercise library to individual workout pages and a plan dashboard, using shared React state and local storage to keep actions in sync.
features: Searchable workout library and exercise details
Daily plan with a five-exercise limit
Persistent plans, sorting, and workout totals

screenshots.title: Explore the library
screenshots.alt: FitLog workout library with search and illustrated exercise cards
screenshots.caption: An exercise library pairs searchable titles with equipment, duration, calories, and rating information.

screenshots.title: Know the movement
screenshots.alt: FitLog exercise details with equipment, sets, reps, and planning actions
screenshots.caption: The detail page puts exercise information beside actions to add it to today's plan or save it for later.

screenshots.title: Start a daily plan
screenshots.alt: FitLog plan dashboard showing zero totals and a helpful empty state
screenshots.caption: The plan starts with a clear empty state. As exercises are added, the dashboard derives totals from shared state.

architecture.title: One source of truth for the plan.
architecture.description: The exercise catalog comes from an API; the personal plan lives in the browser. There is no cloud account synchronization.

nodes.label: 01 / CATALOG
nodes.title: Exercise API
nodes.detail: Next.js fetches the library and passes exercise data to the interface.

nodes.label: 02 / ACTIONS
nodes.title: Search & plan
nodes.detail: Discover, save, add, complete, or remove exercises.

nodes.label: 03 / STATE
nodes.title: React Context
nodes.detail: Shared plan, saved workouts, completion IDs, and derived totals.

nodes.label: 04 / PERSISTENCE
nodes.title: localStorage
nodes.detail: Restore browser data first, then persist later state updates.

architecture.note: Local persistence makes refreshes convenient, but does not transfer plans between browsers or devices.

workflow.title: Explore
workflow.detail: Search exercise names and inspect movement information.

workflow.title: Plan
workflow.detail: Add up to five exercises, with duplicate checks and immediate feedback.

workflow.title: Complete
workflow.detail: Mark exercises as done and review the plan's derived totals.

workflow.title: Resume
workflow.detail: Return in the same browser and restore the saved plan from localStorage.

decisions.title: Keep related actions in shared state
decisions.choice: A Context provider owns the plan, saved exercises, completion IDs, and their actions.
decisions.reason: Cards, details, and the plan page need to reflect the same user choices.
decisions.tradeoff: Context is enough at this scale; a larger application may need more granular subscriptions.

decisions.title: Restore before persisting
decisions.choice: A storageLoaded flag gates writes until the initial localStorage read finishes.
decisions.reason: The initial empty React state should not overwrite an existing saved plan.
decisions.tradeoff: Browser storage still needs defensive parsing and cannot provide cross-device sync.

decisions.title: Derive totals from the plan
decisions.choice: Compute duration and calorie totals from the currently selected exercises.
decisions.reason: Derived values avoid maintaining a second set of totals that can drift out of sync.
decisions.tradeoff: Calorie values are estimates supplied by the catalog, not personalized measurements.

lessons: Sharing state across pages without prop drilling
Coordinating browser storage with React effects
Designing duplicate checks, limits, and empty states
improvements: Defensive storage parsing and state-transition tests
Plan editing and clearer completion progress

name: Movie Explorer
imageAlt: Movie Explorer cinematic homepage with a purple and pink movie theater hero
summary: A cinematic way to discover, search, and learn about TV shows.
evidence: External API integration, title search, and an in-context details modal.
overview: Movie Explorer makes discovering a new show feel as enjoyable as watching one. It brings together a browsable show grid, title search, ratings and release information, and a quick details view, all powered by the TVMaze API.
challenge: Present a large catalog of shows in an experience that feels inviting rather than overwhelming.
solution: I built a responsive, cinema-inspired interface with a clear search flow and a details modal that lets visitors explore a show without losing their place.
features: TV show browsing with TVMaze API data
Ratings, premiere dates, and poster previews
Details modal with genres and summaries
